theme: The Servant’s obedience; the suffering servant
readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 50:1-53:12. This is the heart of the book. The Servant is obedient, beaten, and then, in chapter 53, pierced for our transgressions. Read Isaiah 52:13-53:12 twice. Let the language slow you down.
settingTheScene: These chapters contain the third and fourth Servant Songs. Isaiah 50:4-9 describes the Servant’s willing suffering. Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12 is the most famous passage in the Old Testament about the Messiah’s suffering and death. It was written about 700 years before Jesus. Early Christians, including Philip with the Ethiopian official in Acts 8, took this chapter as the key to understanding the gospel.
observation: “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting” (50:6).
“But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced” (50:7).
“Awake, awake, put on your strength, O arm of the LORD” (51:9).
“How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace” (52:7).
“Behold, my servant shall act wisely; he shall be high and lifted up, and shall be exalted” (52:13).
“He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief” (53:3).
“Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted” (53:4).
“But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed” (53:5).
interpretation:
Chapter 50 gives the Servant’s own voice. He is a disciple who listens, with an ear opened by God, morning by morning. He does not turn back. He gives his back to those who strike, and his face to those who spit. Yet he has set his face like a flint. His trust is in the God who helps him, and so he is not put to shame. The perfect obedience the Servant gives is what Israel never offered.

Chapter 51 and the beginning of 52 contain a great call to awake. God’s arm is stirred as in the days of old, when he cut Rahab in pieces and dried up the sea. And the ransomed of the LORD will return with singing. “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news.” The whole earth will see the salvation of our God.

Then comes the fourth song. It begins with a surprise. The Servant will be “high and lifted up,” language used of God in Isaiah 6. Yet his appearance was marred beyond human semblance. Kings will shut their mouths because of him. Then the confession of the people begins in 53:1. He grew up like a tender plant, with no form or majesty. He was despised, rejected, a man of sorrows. “We esteemed him stricken, smitten by God.” We thought he was being punished for his own sins. But verses 5 and 6 reveal the truth: “He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities.” Everything he suffered was for us. “All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.”

The Servant is silent like a lamb led to the slaughter. He was cut off from the land of the living, assigned a grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death, though he had done no violence. Yet “it was the will of the LORD to crush him.” Out of his anguish he will see light and be satisfied. “By his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities.” He pours out his soul to death, is numbered with the transgressors, bears the sin of many, and makes intercession.
connection: Philip began with Isaiah 53 and told the Ethiopian official the good news about Jesus (Acts 8:32-35). 1 Peter 2:22-25 draws on this chapter for the cross. Matthew 8:17 sees Jesus’ healing as fulfilling “he took our illnesses.” Mark 10:45 says the Son of Man came “to give his life as a ransom for many.” Luke 22:37 quotes “he was numbered with the transgressors.” Romans 5:19 speaks of the many being made righteous through one man’s obedience.
application:
Read Isaiah 53:4-6 aloud and replace “our” with “my.” Let it become personal.

Thank Jesus specifically for one thing he bore for you: your guilt, shame, sorrow, or sickness.

Share the good news of this chapter with someone this week, as Philip did.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being despised and rejected for you.
Tell him what it means that he was pierced for your transgressions.
Ask him to make you trust his healing.
